blocks.prompt: The Wolf Pack Is Just a Family
blocks.text: A wolf pack is not a gang. It is a family. Most packs are just a mom, a dad, and their pups. The pups are born in spring inside a den in the ground. They are born blind. Their eyes open after about two weeks. Every wolf in the family helps feed the pups. When the pups are big enough, they come out and play. They chew on sticks. They pounce on each other. They practice being wolves. At night the whole family howls together. The howl can carry for miles.

blocks.prompt: Why Wolves Howl
blocks.text: A wolf howl is not a spooky sound made for the movies. It is a phone call. Wolves live in families that roam over huge stretches of land. A pack can cross thirty miles in a single day looking for food, so family members get separated. That is when they howl. A howl is low and long, and low, long sounds travel far. In open country a howl can reach other wolves six miles away. The howl carries real information. It says where the wolf is. It also says who the wolf is, because every wolf has its own voice, and packmates can tell each other apart. When the whole family howls at once, they slide their voices up and down instead of matching each other. Researchers think this makes a small pack sound bigger to any stranger listening. Wolves howl for one more reason: to warn other packs to stay off their land. And wolves do not howl at the moon. They howl at night because night is when they travel, and they tilt their heads up because it lifts the sound over the trees.

blocks.prompt: The Hunt That Usually Fails
blocks.text: A wolf is built for the long chase, not the ambush. A cat creeps close and explodes. A wolf does something harder. It runs. Wolves can trot for hours without tiring and can sprint close to thirty five miles an hour in short bursts. Their legs are long, their chests are narrow, and their broad paws splay out on deep snow like snowshoes. The nose does the finding. A wolf can pick up the scent of an elk from more than a mile away when the wind is right. Once the pack locates a herd, the hunt opens with a test. The wolves move at the animals and watch what happens next. A healthy elk stands its ground or runs strong, and a healthy elk can kill a wolf with a single kick to the skull. So the pack reads the herd, looking for the animal that is old, sick, injured, or very young. Most of the time the wolves find nothing worth the risk, and they quit. Biologists who follow packs in Yellowstone have found that the great majority of elk hunts end in failure. A pack may test dozens of animals for every one it catches, and wolves are regularly injured or killed by the prey they chase. This is why a wolf pack is not a gang of killers drifting through the woods. It is a family doing dangerous, exhausting work, and losing far more often than it wins.

blocks.prompt: The Alpha Wolf That Never Existed
blocks.text: In 1970 a biologist named L. David Mech published a book called The Wolf. It was careful, thorough, and enormously popular, and one idea inside it escaped into the world and refused to die: the alpha wolf. The alpha, readers learned, was the wolf that had fought its way to the top of the pack. Below it ranked the betas. At the bottom crouched the omega, the wolf that ate last and took the abuse. The picture was vivid, and it was wrong, and Mech has spent much of his career since then saying so. The trouble was the wolves the idea came from. The dominance research had been done on captive wolves: unrelated adults, collected from different places and dropped together into an enclosure with no way out. Strangers forced into a pen do fight over food and space, and a ranking does emerge. But that is a description of a prison, not of a wolf. When researchers finally spent years watching wild packs, on Ellesmere Island and in Minnesota and later in Yellowstone, the ranking dissolved. A wild pack is almost always a family. It is a breeding pair and their offspring from the last few years. The two wolves in charge are in charge for the same reason your parents are in charge, which is that they are the parents. Nobody fought anyone for the job. The young wolves do not challenge them either. They grow up, leave home, find a mate, and start a family of their own. Mech asked his own publisher to stop printing his book. He has written papers, given talks, and posted videos trying to retire a word he helped release. It has not worked. The alpha wolf lives on in gym slogans and business books and internet advice: a fierce, lonely animal that turned out to be somebody's dad.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Yellowstone's last wolves were killed in the 1920s
31 wolves released in 1995 and 1996
How Wolves Change Rivers: tens of millions of views
Willows recover best where beavers hold water
Wolf carcasses feed ravens, eagles, and bears
Coyote numbers fell, foxes gained

blocks.prompt: The Wolves That Changed the Rivers, or Did They
blocks.text: For seventy years, Yellowstone National Park had no wolves. The last of them were shot and trapped in the 1920s, back when the government paid people to kill predators and the park itself did much of the killing. Then, in 1995 and 1996, biologists captured wolves in Canada, drove them south, and released thirty one of them into the park. What happened next became one of the most famous stories in modern science, and it is worth learning twice: once because parts of it are true, and once because parts of it are not. The story goes like this. With no wolves, elk had grown numerous and comfortable. They stood in the open valleys and along the streams and ate the young willows and aspens down to stubble. Wolves returned, and suddenly an elk could not afford to stand still in an open valley. The elk moved, and they moved away from the places where a wolf could corner them. Released from constant grazing, the willows shot up. Beavers, which need willow, came back and built dams. The dams made ponds, the ponds held fish and birds and frogs, and the roots of the new trees knit the crumbling banks together until the rivers themselves stopped wandering and settled into their channels. A short film called How Wolves Change Rivers set this account to music in 2014, and it has been watched tens of millions of times. It ends by telling you the wolves changed the rivers. Ecologists who have spent their careers in that valley have spent the years since carefully taking the story apart. Elk numbers on the northern range did collapse, from roughly seventeen thousand to a few thousand, but wolves were only one cause. Human hunters killed thousands of elk in those same years, a long drought dried the range, and grizzly bears and cougars, also recovering, took many of the calves. Untangling those causes is genuinely difficult, and no careful scientist hands the wolves all the credit. The willows are the sharper problem. When researchers went out and measured them, they found real recovery in some places and almost none in others. The best predictor of a thriving willow was not the presence of wolves. It was the presence of water, which usually meant a beaver dam. Yellowstone had lost its beavers along with its wolves, and without dams the water table had dropped so far that even an ungrazed willow could not grow tall. The system had not simply been paused by the absence of wolves. It had changed state, and a changed state does not spring back just because the missing piece is put back in the box. As for the rivers, the geologists were blunt: there is little evidence that channels reshaped themselves the way the film describes. So what did the wolves actually do? Real things, measurable ones. They are a large part of why elk no longer loiter in the most dangerous places. They leave carcasses that feed ravens, eagles, bears, magpies, and beetles through the winter. They have pushed coyote numbers down, which appears to have helped foxes and pronghorn fawns. Those are genuine ecological effects and they matter. But the tidy version, the one where a predator returns and a broken world reassembles itself, is a story humans wanted rather than a result nature delivered. It is easy to see why we wanted it. It offers the possibility that our damage is reversible, that we can undo what we did by returning the piece we removed. The Yellowstone data suggests something harder and more useful: it is far cheaper to keep an ecosystem than to rebuild one.
